Photograph: Kin Cheung/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AFP/Getty Images Andy Burnham Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days Exclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster election Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen? Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor Tue 25 Aug 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 18.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission. Burnham, a longtime advocate of electoral reform, will be asked to support the new commission into ditching first past the post in his first 100 days as prime minister. MPs have said the commission must report before the next election and hope to put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission. . New polling of MPs by YouGov suggests the change is now supported by a majority in the Commons. Of those polled, 53% of MPs said they supported a review into first past the post – the current system of voting. An amendment to launch the commission has been backed by 185 MPs, including a number of former ministers and supporters of the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer. Whoever wins today’s elections, democracy is the loser under first past the post | Polly Toynbee Read more The amendment has been tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages on 2 September. A Labour source said: “The representation of the people bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference, and that’s what the government is prioritising. “Andy remains strongly committed to electoral reform, and has indicated this is a matter for a future party manifesto, given a mandate would need to be secured for it.” Burnham endorsed the call for a national commission on electoral reform at last year’s Labour conference, saying then as mayor of Greater Manchester that he backed “a manifesto commitment to a system of proportional representation to be introduced into Westminster elections in the next parliament.” The 98 Labour signatories to the amendment, tabled by Labour’s Alex Sobel include influential backbenchers such as Luke Akehurst and Chris Curtis, leading Labour centrists. Overall, MPs have signed from eight parties, as well as independents. Signatories also include MPs who have recently become ministers and ministerial aides – including the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, communities minister Florence Eshalomi and the prime minister’s parliamentary private secretary and close ally Jo Platt. However, the newly appointed frontbench MPs may by convention withdraw support for backbench amendments once parliament returns. A new commission would not require legislation – meaning the amendment itself may end up out of scope of the bill. But MPs intend to use the amendment as a way of signalling to the prime minister the breadth of support for swifter reform. A national commission could consider a range of other proportional voting systems to replace first past the post, the current system for a general election in the UK which means the winners of the most votes in each constituency are elected. Other systems are used across the UK, including the Scottish parliament, the Welsh parliament and mayoral votes. In Scottish and Welsh elections, there are votes for a candidate and for a party, so additional members can be elected from a list alongside constituency representatives. In the recent Greater Manchester mayoralty, voters were given a first and second choice. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Sobel said it was time for the prime minister to endorse the push – signed by more MPs than any other amendment in parliament. “Now we know a majority of MPs back this proposal, including a majority of Labour MPs. I know the prime minister is committed to reforming our electoral system and I and all the MPs who signed this amendment want to work with him to set the UK on a road towards fair, modern general elections,” he said. MPs told the Guardian that Burnham should announce the commission before the October budget. Rachel Blake, the former Treasury minister, said: “The PLP agrees with Andy Burnham that first past the post is broken, and that a national commission is the way to get a grip on it. The government should press ahead and launch this process within the prime minister’s first hundred days.” Akehurst, a member of Labour’s governing national executive committee, said: “Parliament is catching up with the public, most of whom already support electoral reform. Andy Burnham has a good track record on proportional representation, and it’s now hugely popular across the Labour party. He should seize this opportunity.” Labour MP Lizzi Collinge said first past the post “particularly devalues the votes of renters, young people and BAME people, and delivers parliaments that do not represent what most people voted for.” Another former Labour minister, Catherine Fookes, said first past the post “can’t cope with modern, multiparty politics. Andy Burnham has long talked about the need to move to a fair, proportional system. If he acts now by setting up a commission, he will find that most MPs support him from across parliament – and make good on his promise to rewire British politics.” A sixth Labour MP, Mike Reader, said that the poll of MPs showed there had been “a sea change in support for PR across Labour and the public. Most MPs know it is the fair thing for the country, it’s just a matter of how we get there. We hope Andy Burnham will now stick to his guns.” Labour members at the party’s annual conference in 2022 had previously backed a move towards proportional representation, which Burnham called a “historic vote” and said would be a move towards “a country that works for everybody, where everyone’s vote counts”. Campaign groups said they hoped Burnham would seize the moment for reform while he had a workable parliamentary majority. Make Votes Matter chief executive Emma Harrison said: “I’ve spoken alongside Andy in favour of proportional representation, I know he supports it – now he must show the public he deserves our trust.” The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum was held to ask whether to change to an alternative vote system, where voters rank candidates in order of preference. Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPA View image in fullscreen A woman at a national protest against toxic waste dumping in Zagreb earlier this month. Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPA Waste ‘We don’t have time for more promises’: the Croatian town that took on an illegal waste dump After years of illegal mass flytipping in Gospić, fed-up residents decided to take matters into their own hands Pippa Neill Environment reporter Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “G ospić is our home,” Željka Šikić shouted to a crowd of 40,000 people outside the Croatian parliament earlier this month. The slogan is the name of a campaign she helped to set up to protest against the illegal dumping of waste in Gospić, a town in the mountainous Lika region of central Croatia . Between 2022 and 2024, waste was illegally abandoned at several sites in the town. At one of the biggest, just 50 metres from Šikić’s home, an estimated 35,000 tonnes of waste, some of it hazardous, was dumped and buried. In the dead of night, lorries heaving with waste would pass her front door and enter a nearby industrial site. This activity went largely unnoticed by the local authorities and police. But residents in Gospić were well aware and started taking it in turns to stay up to photograph the vehicles coming in and out of the site. “I don’t think it should be our job to stay awake all night to see what’s going on,” Šikić says. View image in fullscreen An illegal waste site in Gospić in August. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy The waste became a blight on the community and a recent report from the Croatian Institute of Public Health revealed Pfas “forever chemicals” had been detected in groundwater samples nearby. Elevated concentrations of copper and lead were also detected in the soil. Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that have been linked to serious health conditions , including several types of cancer. They are known as “forever chemicals” because of how long they persist in the environment. Despite assurances that their drinking water is safe, a lack of trust means many residents have resorted to buying bottled water. “I’m really scared,” Šikić says. “I would like to move house but I don’t know who would pay for the house on the first road next to the waste. I feel betrayed.” View image in fullscreen Residents took to filming lorries going in and out of one of the dumping sites on the outskirts of Gospić, seen here last month. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy In February 2025, years after the activity began, police and law enforcement officers arrested 13 people on suspicion of being part of the environmental criminal network involved in dumping the waste. The main suspects, two Croatian nationals, were considered high-value targets by Europol and were believed to have orchestrated the illegal import of hazardous waste from Italy, Slovenia and Germany. It is thought the criminals generated upwards of €4m (£3.4m) in profit from this activity. Waste crime is big business. Criminal networks often take advantage of the high costs associated with treating and disposing of waste properly. By falsifying documents to declare the waste as destined for recycling, they can save on the costs and pocket the difference. Residents in Gospić had hoped the arrests would finally mean the site was shut down and cleaned up. But 18 months later, it is still there. Frustrated by the lack of action, Šikić and 16 other residents joined together to form the “Gospić is our home” movement. Ivana Rukavina Sarić, another member of the campaign group, says: “We called people from different professional backgrounds because we knew from the beginning that this would be highly complicated and would need a multi-disciplinary approach.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Having shared information about their struggles online and with Croatian media, Sarić says the campaign turned national, with the group now getting calls daily from other affected communities. “There are so many waste hotspots in the whole of Croatia and so many people facing similar problems. The problem we have in Gospić is the drop of liquid that overflows the glass,” she says. “It’s become a national, even global problem.” Similar dumping has been reported in several other Croatian towns, but the issue extends far beyond national borders. The United Nations estimates that 15% to 30% of EU waste shipments are illegal, and a recent investigation by the Guardian uncovered irrigation canals contaminated with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste exports. View image in fullscreen What began as a small local campaign has grown into a national movement, with thousands attending a demonstration about the issue in Zagreb this month. Photograph: Ronald Gorsic/Cropix/SIPA/Shutterstock Anger at the scale of the problem prompted tens of thousands of people from across Croatia to descend on the capital on 5 September. It is thought there were upwards of 40,000 people marching through Zagreb. “The capital was full,” Sarić says. The group is demanding a comprehensive remediation of the site and the urgent removal of the buried waste. It also wants all known waste hotspots in Croatia to be included in a national waste strategy. The government has opened two public procurement procedures for the removal, disposal or recovery of the waste. But with the waste still there four years since the illegal activity began, and concerns mounting over potential health and environmental impacts, the group plans to head to Brussels where it will protest at the European parliament. “We’ve lost so much time, we don’t have time for more promises,” Sarić says. “We want clear information, clear deadlines and clear action.” The Croatian government did not respond to a request for comment. https://www.dw.com/en/prague-honours-rom.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OW7L Since the end of WWII, the role of Roma resistance fighters was largely unknown Image: Luboš Palata/DW Advertisement For more than half a million Roma in Czechia and Slovakia , October 15, 2026, marks an important milestone. That day, an exhibition on a largely forgotten chapter of Czech history opened at the Museum of the Romani National Revival in Prague. The exhibit explores the role of Czech and Slovak Romani resistance fighters during the Nazi German occupation and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia from 1938 to 1945. Until now, Czech and Slovak Roma appeared in the history of World War II almost exclusively as victims of the Holocaust against Roma and Sinti. In the so-called Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, Nazi Germany murdered approximately 90% of the Czech Roma during World War II. However, what is less well known is that a large number of Czech and Slovak Roma fought against the German occupiers as partisans in resistance groups and as soldiers in the Czechoslovak Underground Army, or Defense of the Nation, ON. The organizers of the exhibition hope that people will bring their children and grandchildren to show that Roma and Sinti have their own heroes Image: Luboš Palata/DW Roma have heroes, too The exhibition at the Museum of the Roma National Movement therefore marks a turning point in how the Roma are viewed during World War II . At least that is the hope of museum director Emil Scuka, a lawyer, former prosecutor and one of the best-known Czech Roma activists. "We were not only victims; we were also heroes," Scuka said in his speech to several hundred attendees at the exhibition opening, most of whom were Roma from Czechia and Slovakia. "Many people, not even among the Roma themselves, are aware that we Roma fought against Nazism," he noted. In his view, "organizing and opening the exhibition was something my generation owed to these Roma heroes and today we are repaying that debt." Scuka called on those present: "Bring your children and grandchildren here so they can see for themselves and realize that the Roma have heroes too!" He also pointed out that this topic had been completely marginalized in Czech and Slovak historical writing for decades and that the Roma had therefore decided on their own to document the fates of their war heroes. The exhibition presents the detailed life stories of 100 of the most significant Roma partisans and Roma soldiers from the Czech underground army and resistance groups who fought against the Nazis. "We found over 1,400 Romani fighters in the archives. From among them, we selected the 100 most interesting stories for this exhibition," said exhibition curator Radoslav Scuka at the opening. Unseen heroes — Sinti and Roma resist Nazis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Groundbreaking research on Roma resistance fighters Among these figures is Anton Facuna, a sergeant in the American intelligence agency Office of Strategic Services (OSS), who was flown to Slovakia in October 1944 on a secret mission. Slovakia had been a puppet state of Hitler from 1939 to 1945. Another is Josef Serinek, known by the nickname "Black Partisan from Vysocina," who managed to escape from the Nazi concentration camp for Roma in Lety and subsequently founded and commanded the large Capajev-Cerny partisan unit in the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands. In 2022, Czech President Milos Zeman posthumously awarded him the Medal for Heroism. Toward the end of his life, Serinek shared his memories with historian Jan Tesar, who later wrote the three-volume book "Ceska cikanska rapsodie", which translates to Czech Gypsy Rhapsody. Except for Tesar's book, the history of Roma resistance against Nazism has not been researched by Czech and Slovak historians to this day. "I am not aware of any scholarly historical work that deals with Roma resistance against Nazism," Prokop Tomek, a historian at the Military History Institute in Prague , told DW. "The number of 1,400 Roma who took part in the fight against Nazism as members of the resistance or in the foreign army does not strike me as an exaggeration and corresponds to the proportion of the Roma population in Czechoslovakia," Tomek said, adding that the "exhibition on the Roma resistance against Nazism during the war is undoubtedly groundbreaking." The life of resistance fighter Anton Facuna is one of around 100 examples on display Image: Luboš Palata/DW Fears of revealing one's Roma identity To this day, many Roma in Czechia and Slovakia do not publicly acknowledge their ethnic identity. This is partly due to experiences with the Holocaust during the Nazi era that have been passed down through generations. Czech historians and politicians continue to debate the extent to which the Czech authorities of the Protectorate were complicit in the extermination of the Czech Roma. However, one thing is certain: the police registration of all Roma, which had been enshrined in law in Czechoslovakia since 1927, facilitated the extermination of the Roma by the German Nazis. According to estimates by the Czech government, approximately 250,000 Roma live in the country today. In the 2021 census, however, only 21,000 people identified as Roma. Of all ethnic groups in Czechia, which has a population of 10 million, the Roma are among the three largest ethnic minorities in terms of numbers. However, they are the most socially disadvantaged, have very little political representation, and are therefore scarcely present in Czech politics.
